defaults.permitted_development: Across Somerset, a dropped kerb is usually governed first by highway consent rather than ordinary householder permitted development. Planning permission is more likely where the access is onto a classified road, the property is heritage-sensitive, the parking area needs major structural work or the hardstanding itself would not satisfy drainage rules. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Somerset, there is no simple height allowance for a dropped kerb. Problems usually arise where the site needs substantial engineered level changes to make vehicle access work.
rules.depth_rules: Across Somerset, there is no national planning depth figure for a dropped kerb, but a shallow frontage can still fail if it leaves cars overhanging the pavement or creates awkward access.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Somerset, separate highway approval is normally required for a new or altered dropped kerb.
rules.roof_rules: Across Somerset, the crossover route concerns the highway edge, not covered parking or entrance structures.
rules.materials_rules: Across Somerset, use the access and the driveway as one design problem: the parking surface should take run-off within the site and be robust enough for regular vehicle use rather than simply creating a widened opening onto the road.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, forming a new vehicular opening can need a closer planning and heritage review where traditional walls, railings, stone kerbs, paving or trees would be altered.
restrictions.listed_building: A new crossing serving a listed building can need listed building consent where boundary walls, gates, steps, railings or other historic fabric are altered.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or planning conditions can remove the simpler householder route for access and boundary works, so the planning status should be checked before relying only on highway approval.

rules.permitted_development: The key approval for a dropped kerb is normally the council or highway authority vehicle-crossing process. Planning permission can still be needed in some cases, especially on classified roads, in conservation areas, for listed buildings or where the frontage parking arrangement is not planning-compliant. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: There is no simple height allowance for a dropped kerb. Problems usually arise where the site needs substantial engineered level changes to make vehicle access work.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth figure for a dropped kerb, but a shallow frontage can still fail if it leaves cars overhanging the pavement or creates awkward access.
rules.boundary_rules: Separate highway approval is normally required for a new or altered dropped kerb.
rules.roof_rules: A dropped kerb does not authorise a car port or canopy. Covered parking features belong under separate planning rules.
rules.materials_rules: Material choice matters because the crossover normally serves a driveway or hardstanding that still has to satisfy drainage and durability requirements. Permeable or well-drained surfacing is usually the safest companion to a new access.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually makes a new access more sensitive where it removes historic boundary features or changes a traditional frontage.

restrictions.conservation_area: Within a conservation area, access works that disturb original walls, railings, kerb lines or planting often receive a more detailed planning and heritage check.
restrictions.listed_building: If the access serves a listed building or involves curtilage walls, gates, piers or historic paving, listed building consent may be needed as well as any highway or planning approval.
